Run
rŭn
v. (to move swiftly; rendering Hebrew ruts, Greek trecho)
Old English rinnan. Scripture's runners include messengers, prodigals' fathers, and every saint entered in the race set before us.

Biblical Definition

To run is to move at full stretch, and the New Testament makes it the church's athletic figure: “let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus” (Heb 12:1–2). Paul disciplines the figure — “So run, that ye may obtain” (1Co 9:24) — a race is not a stroll. The prophet promises the running strength renewed: “they shall run, and not be weary” (Isa 40:31); the psalmist locates the track: “I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart” (Psa 119:32).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines run as to move swiftly, so that both feet leave the ground at once — haste with the whole body; Scripture's concern is the direction and the endurance.

expand to see more

RUN, v.i. To move or pass swiftly; to hasten in motion.

2. To contend in a race.

3. To flow; to move in a current, as a liquid.

Key Scripture

Heb 12:1 — "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,"

1Co 9:24 — "Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain."

Isa 40:31 — "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint."

Psa 119:32 — "I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart."

Modern Corruption

Hustle culture baptized — running as identity, burnout as devotion — while the biblical race runs with patience, on a set course, looking at a fixed point that is not the runner.

expand to see more

Hebrews' race has three features modern striving lacks: it is set before us (the course is assigned, not invented), it is run with patience (endurance, not sprint-and-collapse), and it is run looking unto Jesus (the eyes are off the runner). Religious hustle keeps the exertion and loses all three — self-chosen course, unsustainable pace, eyes on the metrics. That race has no finish line because it has no author and finisher.

Psalm 119:32 supplies the physiology of holy running: I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart. Obedience at speed is not willpower but cardiac capacity, and God is the one who enlarges. Isaiah's runners likewise wait upon the LORD before they run without weariness — the stillness is the fuel of the speed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ruts (H7323), to run — messengers, warriors, and the strong man of Psalm 19 rejoicing to run his race; Greek trecho (G5143), to run, Paul's favorite athletic verb.

expand to see more

Hebrew ruts (H7323) — to run; which rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race (Psa 19:5).

Greek trecho (G5143) — to run; 1 Corinthians 9:24, Hebrews 12:1, Galatians 5:7 — ye did run well; who did hinder you?

Usage

"“Let us run with patience the race that is set before us” — assigned course, enduring pace, fixed gaze."

"“So run, that ye may obtain” — the race is real and the prize is worth training for."

"“I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart” — God supplies the cardiac capacity."
